The compressor was designed under a NASA Research Announcement (NRA) contract with 2/3 funding from NASA and 1/3 from UTRC.
The design target was to increase efficiency at higher work factor while reducing the maximum diameter of the stage.
Certain key design parameters were fixed, including impeller tip diameter, impeller rotational speed, and impeller inlet hub and shroud radii.
The final compressor design had a pressure ratio of 4.68, work factor of 0.81, and design exit corrected flow rate of 3 lbm/s.
The measured polytropic efficiency was 85.5% and the stall margin was 7.5% at the design flow rate and speed.
The measured efficiency and stall margin were lower than pre-test CFD predictions by 2.4 percentage points and 4.5 percentage points, respectively.

Post-test CFD analysis indicated that the performance differences were likely due to unfavorable unsteady impeller-diffuser interactions, an impeller-diffuser flow rate mismatch, and potential flow separation in the radial-to-axial bend.
Inconsistencies in the implementation of a widely used two-equation turbulence model were identified, and the need for longer integration times in unsteady CFD simulations was highlighted.

Recommended design changes included redesigning the diffuser to eliminate the flow rate mismatch and optimize the vane geometry, as well as redesigning the radial-to-axial bend to minimize flow separation.
Testing the impeller with a vaneless diffuser was recommended to further evaluate the impeller-diffuser interactions.
The mechanical design included detailed structural analyses for low-cycle fatigue, high-cycle fatigue, and burst margin, as well as Campbell diagrams to assess potential resonance issues.
The fabrication process involved careful control of the impeller runouts, imbalance, and blade tip/hub profile measurements.
The diffuser and exit guide vane were assembled as a subassembly and then integrated with the shroud using a holding fixture.

The test instrumentation included steady-state measurements of pressure, temperature, and flow rate, as well as high-response pressure transducers to capture the unsteady impeller-diffuser interactions.
The data reduction methodology included the calculation of performance parameters such as pressure ratio, efficiency, and stall margin.
